stimulus.text:
The Security Council as designed in the United Nations Charter, signed June 26, 1945.

| Members | Who they were | Power |
| 5 permanent members | United States, Soviet Union, Britain, France, China | Any one could veto a Council decision |
| 6 rotating members | Elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms | Voted, but held no veto |
stimulus.source_note: Table drawn from the design of the United Nations Charter (San Francisco, June 1945): five permanent members with the veto and six elected members in the original Council. The elected membership grew to ten in 1965.

source: original; stimulus drawn from book-grounded paraphrases, tables, and photographs (see source_note)
stem: What did the veto power mean for the Security Council?

options.text: The General Assembly could overrule any Council decision
options.misconception: The General Assembly could discuss and recommend, but it could not overrule the Council.

options.text: The Council could act only when all nations agreed
options.misconception: Only the five permanent members held the veto; the rotating members did not.

options.text: Any one permanent member could block a Council decision
The Council could veto the decisions of member nations
options.misconception: The veto blocked the Council itself, not the decisions of individual nations.

rationales.A: Background from the books: the General Assembly could discuss and recommend, but it could not overrule the Council.
rationales.B: Background from the books: only the five permanent members held the veto; the rotating members did not.
rationales.C: The table says any one permanent member could veto a Council decision, so a single great power could stop the Council from acting.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the veto blocked the Council itself, not the decisions of individual nations.
rationales.general:
1. The table gives the five permanent members the power to veto a Council decision.
2. A veto means one member alone can block action, even if all the others agree.
3. Background: the veto was meant to keep the great powers inside the United Nations, since none would join a body that could act against it.
4. The cost was clear: the Council could be frozen whenever the great powers disagreed.
Remember: a veto trades action for membership, since no great power joins a club that can rule against it.
